extracted.intended_audience: registered apprenticeship program sponsors, participating employers, State Apprenticeship Agencies (SAAs), State/local educational agencies, institutions of higher education, apprentices, industry groups, trade associations, and other public commenters on the Department's NPRM and associated information collections
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for submitting public comments on the Department of Labor's proposed rule for registered apprenticeship and CTE apprenticeship, with emphasis on information-collection requests, regulatory costs and burdens on small entities, and alternatives analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desired Focus — necessity and practical utility of the collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the Agency, including whether the information has practical utility;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department is soliciting comments on whether each proposed information collection is necessary to perform agency functions and whether the information collected will have practical utility. Commenters should explain how the information would or would not be useful in practice and provide examples if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desired Focus — accuracy of burden estimates and methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the accuracy of the Department's estimate of the burden related to the IC, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used in the estimate;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters should critique the Department's burden estimates, identify any incorrect assumptions or missing cost categories, suggest alternative parameter values or methods, and provide data or evidence supporting revised estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desired Focus — methods to enhance quality, utility, and clarity of information
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggest methods to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific recommendations for improving the content, format, instructions, or definitions in the proposed collections so responses are clearer, more comparable, or more useful for the Agency's purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desired Focus — minimizing respondent burden and use of technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimize the burden of the IC on those who are to respond, including through the use of appropriate automated, electronic, mechanical, or other technological collection techniques or other forms of IT (e.g., permitting electronic submission of responses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend concrete ways to reduce time/cost burdens (e.g., electronic submissions, pre-filled fields, reduced frequency, streamlined reporting), and, where possible, estimate burden reductions from such changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act compliance requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A Federal agency may not conduct or sponsor a collection of information unless it is approved by OMB under the PRA and displays a currently valid OMB control number. The public also is not required to respond to a collection of information unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number. No person will be subject to penalty for failing to comply with a collection of information if the collection of information does not display a currently valid OMB control number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments may address PRA procedural compliance (submission to OMB, display of control number), and whether the Agency's ICRs meet statutory PRA requirements (see 44 U.S.C. 3501 et seq., and 44 U.S.C. 3512).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for assessing significant economic impact on small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the proposed rule would have a significant economic impact on small entities by dividing the estimated first-year cost and the annualized cost per sponsor (discounted at a 7-percent rate) by the average annual receipts per firm in the industry; significant impact is identified as 3 percent or more of receipts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department's approach: compute first-year and annualized costs per sponsor (7% discount rate), divide by average receipts to get percent-of-receipts; compare to 3% threshold. Commenters should challenge assumptions, alternate thresholds, discount rates, or the choice of average receipts if warranted, and provide alternative calculations or data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of whether a substantial number of small entities are affected
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether affected firms constitute a 'substantial number' of small entities by dividing the number of firms in each size category by the total number of small firms in the industry and reporting the percent (examples: 24.3%, 25.0%, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters can dispute whether the percentage of affected firms constitutes a 'substantial number' for RFA purposes, propose alternative benchmarks, or provide industry-specific context showing why a given percentage is or is not substantial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of industry-specific small business size standards in impact analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the relevant Small Business Size Standard for each industry when assessing impacts (exhibits show standards such as $9.0 million–$47.0 million, $8.5 million–$47.0 million, $8.0 million–$47.0 million for particular NAICS sectors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments should verify the applicable size standards used, suggest corrections if wrong, and discuss how different size standard thresholds would change the distribution of affected firms and the RFA analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-estimation transparency and per-sponsor calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide transparent, component-level cost estimates across years and compute per-sponsor costs by dividing total annual costs by the number of registered apprenticeship program sponsors; report first-year and annualized costs (7% discount rate, 10-year annualized figures used in examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NPRM includes tables breaking down costs by component (rule familiarization, OJT documentation, wage analysis, data reporting, registration, standards adoption, end-point assessments, recordkeeping, program reviews) and by year; commenters should verify component inclusions/exclusions, per-unit cost assumptions, sponsor counts, discounting, and provide corrected tables or alternative approaches if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration and evaluation of regulatory alternatives to minimize impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the RFA, agencies must assess impacts of regulatory alternatives on small entities and consider ways to minimize those impacts; the Department considered two alternatives (remove end-point assessments; conduct program reviews only for cause) and estimated cost reductions for each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters should propose other lower-cost alternatives that would mitigate small business impacts while maintaining program goals, supply cost estimates for those alternatives, and explain how alternatives would preserve program quality/accountability. The Department's rationale for rejecting alternatives (e.g., end-point assessments are key to quality; periodic reviews detect noncompliance) can be challenged with evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of voluntariness in assessing affected population for CTE apprenticeship
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation in CTE is voluntary; therefore only small entities that choose to participate would experience an economic impact—significant or otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments may argue that voluntary participation affects the scope of the RFA analysis (e.g., estimate likely take-up rates, differential impacts on those who opt in), and provide data on expected participation to refine impact estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program review frequency and justification (five-year cycle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department believes all registered apprenticeship programs should be reviewed over a 5-year period as specified in the proposed rule to ensure quality and detect programs needing review; this 5-year period balances resource availability and burden on programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters should evaluate whether a 5-year universal review cycle is necessary, whether for-cause reviews would suffice, estimate cost and detection trade-offs, and provide data or alternative review schedules (e.g., risk-based sampling) that could reduce burden while maintaining oversight.
